The cascade finished in 19.3 seconds against 61.7 seconds: 69% less time, or about 3.2 times faster. Clairic and Clef handled extraction and the decision in under a second combined, where GLM-5.3 took 38 seconds for the same two steps. It also costs 49% less to use the cascaded pipeline vs the all-LLM pipeline. With GLM, both pipelines got the facts and the decision right in every run, but Clairic's repair estimate was identical each time, while GLM-5.3's changed on every run ($250, $250 and $220, with different ranges each time).

Notably, under the all-LLM pipeline both Gemma 4 and Qwen failed at this task, as they were unable to deduce values like repair_cost from the inputs, showing how LLMs are not great at data extraction tasks.

Preview release

Today, we're releasing a hosted endpoint for Clairic on Workers AI. We intend to release the model with open weights soon. We wanted to take the time first to introduce the concept of a System One extraction model, so you can start thinking about how this class of model would fit into appropriate workflows.

The current endpoint is an early checkpoint and we expect it to get better. Here are our early impressions:

  • Reading is strong, but multi-step arithmetic isn't yet. One- and two-step calculations (totals, differences, conversions, date arithmetic) seem reliable. Longer chains of dependent steps are hard for any one-pass model without a scratchpad. The same goes for aggregating across many rows of a table. At least for now, have Clairic predict the value and let code do the math.
  • Estimates need evidence. Clairic estimates best from comparables, history, or descriptive text in the input. Asking it for a value it has no evidence for may be limited in specificity.
  • Calibration is measured, not guaranteed. Intervals are trained to be calibrated and are on most held-out sets, but they can run narrow on unfamiliar data.
  • Forecasting is basic. The model is not designed to accurately replace or predict time-series models that are trained on specific data. You should use it where appropriate, such as non-critical, general pattern matching, not detailed long-horizon forecasting.
  • Use confidence. The architecture makes every answer well formed, not necessarily correct. Use confidence, p_null and the intervals to decide what to automate (in an appropriate workflow context) and what to send off for additional review.

We'll keep working on the arithmetic, estimation and forecasting sides of the model with each checkpoint. After some more work, we plan to release the model open-weights for everyone to play around with as well.

Try it out

Clairic is available as a preview on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic. Call it from a Worker with env.AI.run(), or from anywhere with the REST API. We have full model docs here, as well as a new docs explainer on how the extraction model API looks.

P.S. Since you liked the etymology of the name Clef, here’s how we landed on the name Clairic. We started with a desire to keep the name of the model thematically and sonically similar to Clef. Clair came to mind, sharing the same “cl” sound, as well as roots in music (“Clair de Lune”). More importantly, we wanted the name to be descriptive to the nature of the model. The Clairic model should be able to help you with clerical tasks like extracting data clearly from a corpus of inputs and upholding accuracy in tasks like bookkeeping. The prediction aspect of the model leans into the “Clair” root — allowing you to estimate and predict future values, similar to clairvoyance. Lastly, we like the idea of having this be [Cl]oudflare’s [AI R]egression model. Thus, Clairic was born into the world. We hope you enjoy it.

item.title: Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities
item.description: CVE-2026-88771 lets attackers run commands on NetScaler Gateway before anyone signs in. Patching takes time most teams don't have, so the sign-in decision has to move in front of the vulnerable code.
item.dc:creator: Grant Bourzikas
Kenny Johnson
item.content:encoded:
The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server. Indeed, the disclosures included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in. As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their users’ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update.

If you’re a NetScaler customer and you haven’t patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one. Once you’ve finished the patch, we’ll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls.

This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server?

Citrix released software updates to address the flaw, and Cloudflare followed with an emergency web application firewall (WAF) rule on October 1. But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful — it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely don’t care about your security patch.

Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but it’s reactive and does not account for the next exploit that’s discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. That’s why it is crucial to build defense in depth, to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue.

Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform.

The NetScaler exploit

Citrix's September 27, 2026 bulletin reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3 and October 8 addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks.

CISA's alert and Mandiant's technical investigation cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771.

In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. The gateway validates the ticket before proxying the desktop connection. Citrix documents these as distinct stages of the connection workflow. The entire exploit stems from the fact that the Gateway has to be publicly accessible on the Internet, otherwise users would not be able to initiate their desktop connection.

Put the access decision in front of the authentication server

The best thing that you can do, after patching all your instances, is move any publicly accessible login pages or applications behind single sign-on before the request ever hits the target server. Cloudflare Access can enforce an independent access policy before the request reaches the existing gateway server. The Citrix environment continues to determine which desktop the user may launch and to validate the resulting session ticket. The additional boundary ensures that an attacker could never get to the Gateway server to try running specific exploits. They would only see the Cloudflare Access login page.

That decision no longer depends on recognizing an exploit signature and blocking that way, but rather on a set of Zero Trust policies that determine if someone should even be there to begin with. More attacks like this are coming, and adopting Zero Trust controls throughout your network is the single most important thing you should do next.

This follows the principle described in Cloudflare's own architecture as customer zero: reduce exposure and use independent defenses so that one flaw does not become a compromise. Here, the practical starting point is the service that users reach before they enter their applications.

Protecting the web authentication path adds a boundary in front of the existing Citrix controls. It does not automatically extend that boundary to other gateway services, including DTLS-enabled listeners. Those interfaces still need their own exposure review and applicable security updates, even when the desktop sessions they support already require authentication.

The origin connection must enforce the same boundary

Changing a DNS record and enforcing Access policies are not enough. If an attacker can connect to the original address or an alternate hostname, they can avoid the controls placed in front of it. Access enforces a specific hostname: if the authentication server can be reached via an IP address or alternative hostname, then the Access policy enforcement is worthless. It’s important to take steps to ensure that all traffic comes from a request that was validated by Access. There are a few different approaches to accomplish this, based on your internal architecture.

Cloudflare Tunnel is the most commonly used approach. It establishes an outbound only tunnel from your application server and allows you to close all inbound IP traffic. This means that you won’t have a public IP for the server that can be reached by anyone.

When a public origin IP Address must remain or connector software cannot be run, network restrictions and origin authentication need to constrain the connections it accepts. For example, Dedicated CDN Egress IPs give an account dedicated source addresses for traffic from Cloudflare to its origins. The application server’s firewall can allow those addresses and reject other sources. This makes the network restriction specific to the account's traffic, rather than broadly allowing traffic from Cloudflare's shared address ranges.

Authenticated Origin Pulls can add further depth with mutual TLS to verify the Cloudflare-to-origin connection.

An origin that supports it can also validate the Access JSON Web Token, including its signature, issuer, expiry, and intended application audience. This is the best way to guarantee that a request was authenticated by Access.

If you're unsure where to start, speak with a Cloudflare expert to review your architecture and identify which controls fit your environment.

Protect the web-facing authentication service

Cloudflare Access determines who may reach the web application; Cloudflare's web application firewall (WAF) inspects HTTP requests to that same protected service. The WAF runs before any Access authentication checks, which gives you the ability to completely block known malicious IPs, specific countries, ASNs, or other attributes you know definitely shouldn’t be accessing your applications. The firewall runs continuously on all requests and will also identify users who managed to authenticate attempting to run exploits with known CVE signatures.

Alongside managed CVE signatures, WAF Attack Score uses machine learning to identify potentially malicious requests that do not exactly match a known rule. Administrators can use the score in rules that block or challenge requests. The WAF attack score is powered by network observations from Cloudflare's global network traffic and Cloudforce One investigations feed Cloudflare's shared threat-intelligence platform.

Customers with a Cloudforce One threat intelligence subscription can also use live threat indicators in WAF policies. That adds context about known malicious sources alongside inspection of the request itself.

Reducing exposure does not remove an attacker who already has a foothold. Seriously: go patch your system if you haven’t, and follow Citrix's suspected-compromise guidance. They lay out how to preserve evidence, revoke credentials and certificates, investigate connected systems, and rebuild or restore from a known-good state.

Extend Zero Trust to desktop access, or remove the desktop dependency

Protecting web authentication can be an initial step without making it the final architecture. Cloudflare's Zero Trust architecture for virtual desktops also supports controlling access to the desktop infrastructure itself. With the Cloudflare One Client and private-network connectivity, teams can restrict who and which devices may reach the endpoints carrying desktop traffic, including an existing Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) path. This requires its own routing and policy design; it is not a capability supplied by the browser authentication proxy alone.

Some workflows can remove the ICA dependency instead. For supported Windows workloads,  Cloudflare's browser-based remote desktop access connects users to a Windows host through Cloudflare Tunnel, without a local remote desktop client. If users only need a desktop to open web applications, Access and Browser Isolation can replace that web-access use case without a full virtual desktop.

Start by protecting the authentication service and existing desktop connections. Then replace virtual desktops used only for web access, and move supported Windows workflows to browser-based remote desktops. Reducing exposure does not have to wait for a full desktop migration.

Decide which authentication services need to be public

The same assessment applies beyond virtual desktops. An employee portal or management console may need to be reachable by approved users from anywhere, without needing to accept application requests from everyone.

Not every authentication page can require a prior employee identity. Consumer login pages and the identity-provider endpoints required to establish an initial session may need to remain publicly reachable. Protect those intentionally, and avoid introducing circular authentication dependencies. The point is to make reachability a design decision rather than an inherited default.

Start with one restricted service. Map the web and non-web paths into it, then put the access decision ahead of its authentication surface. Before expanding the rollout, validate the boundary in your own environment:

  1. Request the protected hostname without signing in. Confirm the request stops at Cloudflare rather than reaching the origin.
  2. Sign in with a test account outside the permitted group. Confirm it still cannot reach the protected application.
  3. Test direct-origin addresses and alternate hostnames. Confirm none bypasses the access policy.
  4. Sign in as an approved user. Confirm authentication, desktop launch, and session reconnection still work.

Check the relevant policy, firewall, and origin logs rather than relying only on what the browser displays. Repeat these checks when routing, identity, or failover settings change, so the next configuration update does not quietly reopen the path you closed.

Bring the controls together

The full architecture brings the access decision, web inspection, and availability controls in front of NetScaler, with restrictions on the connection to the origin. The public origin and Tunnel paths are alternatives. The native desktop connection remains separate, with an optional Zero Trust network access layer around that traffic.

Get started

Speak with a Cloudflare expert to plan the right controls for your environment. Download the solution brief and sign up for the upcoming webinar.

Andrei Migia, Nathan Sackett, and Doug Shepherd contributed to this post.

item.title: Continuous accountability for Verified bots
item.description: Identity alone doesn't guarantee a bot will behave responsibly. We are introducing a system to continuously evaluate whether Verified bots honor site preferences, like robots.txt and HTTP 429s, ensuring they remain accountable over time.
item.dc:creator: Chris Tsoukaladelis
item.content:encoded:
A driver’s license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether they’ll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next. A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. It’s not always malicious — often it’s just a misconfiguration or a bug.

As we described in a previous blog post on bot behavior, we strive to verify two questions: “Are you who you say you are?” and “Can we trust you?” To be a Cloudflare Verified Bot, you broadly need to meet three criteria:

  1. Identify yourself accurately and securely
  2. Do only what you say you will do
  3. Don’t engage in abusive behavior

Bots use Web Bot Auth to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBase then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm.

Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when Verified bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to “Can we trust you?” remains “Yes.”

This is where the distinction between risk and trust becomes important:

  • Risk describes the likelihood that a particular request or point-in-time action may be harmful, and it can change from one moment to the next.
  • Trust is built over time through repeated and consistent behavior.

For example, we de-listed Perplexity’s bot from our Verified bot list in 2025 when it sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attempted to circumvent controls when those requests were blocked.

Do not engage in abusive behavior

This simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement. When crawlers don’t respect site preferences, that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust.

We developed a system to measure how often a crawler respects site preferences. These observations will translate to an explainable trust band: a range showing how consistently a bot respects site preferences and which observed behaviors informed that assessment, rather than a permanent judgment about a bot or its operator. The initial signals we evaluate are:

  • Does the bot respect instructions?
  • Did it respond to direct feedback?

We consider these to be “common sense” rules, a courtesy to the operators who provide the information bots seek. In the future, we will be sharing these scores publicly on Radar, as well as expanding the ways we measure. This score gives responsible bot operators a way to demonstrate that trust is being upheld over time. Verify, but continuously re-verify.

When in Rome, do as the Romans do

A robots.txt file is the primary way to communicate site owner preferences. Our system considers whether a bot’s observed traffic is consistent with those published preferences over time.

Robots.txt tells all (or specific) bots to only crawl specific parts of a website. Isolated violations and other types of one-offs may not be significant. What we look for instead are repeated patterns of behavior that disregards site preferences. The expectation is simply for responsible bots to consult and honor the preferences that websites publish, in line with RFC 9309.

And just to be clear, a robots.txt sets the minimum rules for what bots and agents should not do. But there is no implication that anything not stated is allowed. For example, a robots.txt does not need to say that a bot must stop when the site can communicate that continued access is unwelcome through other signals.

What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others

Bots can remain entirely within allowed paths while still placing substantial load on the websites they visit. One of the clearest ways a website can push back is with an HTTP 429 (“Too Many Requests”) response. A 429 is a directive for the visitor to reduce its request rate, sometimes with guidance about how long to wait before trying again.

Our system considers whether the bot’s traffic adapts after receiving that signal. Does it slow down, pause, or does it continue sending requests at the same pace? We then incorporate that behavior into the bot’s trust band over time: consistently slowing down or pausing increases trust, while repeatedly ignoring the signal lowers it.

Building trust over time

Observing these signals is only a first step toward making verified automation accountable over time. By pairing bot identity with evidence of continuing behavior, we can give site owners more confidence that the bots they choose to allow are respecting their preferences, give bot operators a way to demonstrate they deserve trust, and provide context to website owners about the automated traffic reaching them.

This system, alongside Bot Preference Sync and Bot Management, forms an accountability loop for automated traffic. Bot Preference Sync helps website owners publish their preferences, and observing how bots interact with these preferences shows whether Verified bots consistently honor them over time. Bot Management lets website owners decide how that traffic is handled. Together, they help ensure that trust is earned through transparent, accountable behavior, not assumed from identity alone.

We are already using this system internally to evaluate how consistently Verified bots honor website preferences. Because trust is built over time, we assess sustained patterns rather than isolated events. We are using this initial phase to build that history and refine how those observations become useful guidance. Building on that foundation, we plan to make the system available to all Cloudflare customers, who will be able to choose the trust threshold used to decide how Verified bot traffic is handled. Our goal is straightforward: to keep website preferences meaningful, and ensure trust is earned through sustained behavior.

Want to learn more about how you can handle bots? Cloudflare customers can already use Bot Management to manage automated traffic and Bot Preference Sync to align their published preferences with their configured policies. To explore the ever-growing Verified bot population, see the trends on Radar.

And if you are interested in helping build the future of bot identity and accountability, explore open roles at Cloudflare.

item.title: A fully programmable secure web gateway
item.description: Cloudflare Gateway and Data Loss Prevention have inherited the flexibility and power of Cloudflare Workers through our full-stack integration with the Cloudflare Developer platform.
item.dc:creator: AJ Gerstenhaber
Abe Carryl
item.content:encoded:
Every secure web gateway on the market works the same way: traffic matches a condition. A terminal action fires. Allow, Block, Isolate, Log. This model has been the foundation of network security for nearly 30 years, and it handles the common case well. But it has a ceiling, and customers with complex environments hit that ceiling regularly.

Earlier this year, we shared our vision to build a truly programmable SASE platform. We also outlined how the term programmability has become diluted by the security industry. Most vendors claim programmability because they have public APIs, Terraform providers, webhooks, and alerting. Cloudflare offers all of those things too, but that’s not enough. True programmability means running your own code — arbitrary logic that you wrote for your specific environment — inline in the policy evaluation path, at the moment a security decision is made.

Today, we’re excited to announce Cloudflare is bringing true programmability to Cloudflare Gateway and DLP (Data Loss Prevention) by integrating it with the entirety of our edge computing platform. We are releasing a new type of Gateway action, Forward, and custom validation functions, available to all Zero Trust plans. These capabilities allow you to use a Cloudflare Worker to transform and manipulate traffic, or to bring your own data to policy evaluation.

The trade-off that every security team faces

For as long as firewalls have existed, businesses have faced a binary choice. You can maintain your own security detection engine — your own firewall, your own proxy infrastructure — with high maintenance overhead and low portability, in exchange for maximum customization. Or, you can accept the constraints of a vendor, offloading the considerable maintenance cost, at the expense of flexibility to solve problems specific to your environment.

In six years of building Cloudflare Gateway, we have heard from thousands of customers struggling with this trade-off. A security team migrating access controls for a critical internal application needs to inject HTTP headers based on JSON Web Token (JWT) claims from their identity provider. The data exists in the request context, but Gateway cannot read the JWT and write the header. So the team stands up a pool of NGINX proxies solely to perform this transformation. That infrastructure now must be patched, monitored, and secured... indefinitely.

Another team wants a Slack notification the moment an employee signs up for a new SaaS service. The policy engine can detect the sign-up event, but it can only Allow or Block. So the team builds a Logpush-to-SIEM-to-Slack pipeline with a 5 to 15 minute delay and no guarantee of delivery. And piles on yet another piece of infrastructure.

Dozens of enterprise customers have asked for warning pages that prompt users for justification before allowing access to sensitive destinations. Most then want to customize the ensuing behavior based on additional context about who the user is and the level of access requested. But serving customized, dynamic responses from a policy engine is exceedingly difficult.

We have offered customers many extension points over the years. But along with every other firewall vendor, it is impossible to build features to cover threat vectors as quickly as they can appear. However, we also recognize that the best solutions are those which are infinitely extensible to your environment.

Why only Cloudflare can solve this problem

Cloudflare is not just a firewall, or a secure web gateway, a content delivery network, or an edge service. Cloudflare is a composable compute platform. Cloudflare Workers already allows customers to run complex logic on our network edge from any of our 330+ locations worldwide. Cloudflare Gateway already evaluates and enforces security policy on user traffic at those same locations, on the same machines, in the same data centers.

Only Cloudflare runs both distributed customer compute and a full-featured secure web gateway and firewall in the same globally distributed network. We have the unique opportunity and ability to combine those functions into the industry’s first completely programmable and customizable SASE platform.

Gateway and Workers were built on the same infrastructure from the beginning. When Gateway forwards traffic to a Worker, that dispatch is a local function call. There is no hairpinning. There is no additional latency from crossing a network boundary. This is the first time that customers will have absolute control over how their proxied traffic is processed, without compromise, using code that they can write and execute without maintaining any sort of infrastructure.

Standalone SASE providers without their own compute platform require you to deploy automation in a separate cloud, manually configure webhooks, and accept the round-trip latency and management overhead of stitching together disconnected systems. No other vendor in this space has a programmable edge compute platform co-located with their security gateway. As threats advance at AI-powered speed, this will provide much needed flexibility and agility for security organizations.

Two Gateway entry points: Forward action and Custom Functions

A new Gateway action type called Forward and a new policy resource called a Custom Function are two distinct ways to call a Worker from a Gateway policy. The Forward action is available in public beta today, and Custom Functions will be available before the end of the year.

Forward action: traffic transformation and proxy

You can customize HTTP traffic behavior with a new policy action called Forward that routes the matched HTTP request to a Worker as a proxy. Policies with the Forward action are evaluated for traffic allowed by HTTP policies. The first matching Forward rule will then be applied to your traffic, and the traffic will be sent to its bound Cloudflare Worker. The Worker acts as inline middleware: it receives the full headers and request body. Your logic can then choose to modify either one (or take another asynchronous action of some kind), forward the request to the origin, receive the response, can modify that too, and return the final response to the user.

import { WorkerEntrypoint } from "cloudflare:workers";
import type {
  GatewayMiddlewareContext,
  GatewayMiddlewareNext,
} from "@cloudflare/zt-types";

export class GatewayMiddleware extends WorkerEntrypoint {
  async handle(
    request: Request,
    context: GatewayMiddlewareContext,
    next: GatewayMiddlewareNext,
  ): Promise<Response> {
    // Read a value from the Gateway context
    const clientIP = context.srcIp;

    // Add headers before the request reaches the origin
    request.headers.set("X-Gateway-Client-IP", clientIP);

    // Forward upstream and get the response
    const response = await next(request);

    // Modify the response before it reaches the user
    response.headers.set("X-Processed-By", "gateway-middleware");

    return response;
  }
}

Gateway handles the TCP connections, TLS termination and re-encryption, certificate management, and HTTP version negotiation. The Worker is responsible only for the transformation logic. You get a customizable, proxy-like extension point for your existing security stack, with none of the operational cost of hosting a traditional HTTP proxy.

Your Workers also do not have to transform the request. A rule's sole purpose can be to proxy a request to a Worker that receives the full context of the matched request asynchronously: send a Slack message, write to R2, log to an external pipeline, call a webhook, update a KV store. The traffic can continue to its destination, unbothered.

Custom functions: inline policy evaluation

A custom function calls out to a Worker inline during Gateway policy evaluation and returns a value. The function is then exposed as a selector in the Gateway policy builder, and the selector is evaluated against its values. The selector is usable in the condition of any network or HTTP Gateway rule, the same way a built-in selector like Source IP or Content Category works today.

The Worker receives context about the request: source IP, destination, user identity, device posture, HTTP headers, and more, depending on the policy phase. The Worker returns a typed value (string, number, or boolean) that Gateway uses in rule conditions. The contract is simple: data in, value out.

Here is a custom function that parses a JWT Authorization header and returns the user's role:

export class GatewayCustomSelector extends WorkerEntrypoint {
  async compute(ctx: GatewayContext): Promise<string> {
    const authHeader = ctx.request.headers.get("Authorization");
    if (!authHeader) return "anonymous";

    const token = authHeader.replace("Bearer ", "");
    const payload = JSON.parse(atob(token.split(".")[1]));
    return payload.groups?.[0] ?? "unknown";
  }
}

With this function deployed, an administrator can create an HTTP policy rule: Custom Function "JWT Role" contains "finance_contractor" with an action of Allow. The custom function becomes part of the rule condition, evaluated alongside every other selector.

Custom functions are not limited to HTTP traffic. Because they receive identity, device posture, and connection metadata instead of the full HTTP request, you can use them in the Gateway Network policy rule builder with arbitrary Layer 4 port and protocol traffic as well.

The Worker itself can do anything a Worker can already do — call external APIs, read from KV or D1, or invoke Workers AI. But from Gateway's perspective, the function is deterministic: data in, value out.

When to use a custom function or a Forward action

Custom functions are designed for quick, bounded, stateless evaluations of data which can return a shaped response. You should think of their use similarly to data that can already be evaluated in Gateway selectors; that is, calculations on data that exist within a set of criteria, e.g. “Ports within this range,” or “URL paths that match this regex pattern.” The power comes from being able to extend your structured evaluations with arbitrary or internal sources of data, for which you’ll see some examples below.

The Forward action requires a little more planning and preparation. It can be used for powerful transformations inline with users’ live requests, and can manipulate them in complex ways both on the egress and return to the origin service. These should be thought of as transformation functions, something that very few enterprise security proxies even conceptualize today. Workers that use the Forward action should be targeted and designed carefully to avoid adverse effects on the end user’s overall experience.

What you can build

Purpose justification and interstitial pages

A Worker intercepts a request to a sensitive destination and returns an interstitial page requiring the end user to provide a written justification for access. The Worker calls Cloudflare KV to write a session with a TTL, so the user is only prompted once per configured period. It writes the user's identity and their stated justification to Cloudflare D1, creating an audit trail. Or, you can use Hyperdrive to write that record to any internal database you already operate.

This has been one of our most-requested features for over four years. With a Worker able to process and manipulate HTTP traffic, it's easy to build to your own standards.

Dynamic HTTP header injection

A custom function parses a JWT from the request's Authorization header, extracts the user's role or group membership, and returns it as a selector value. A Gateway rule matches on that value and sets an X-App-Role header on the upstream request. No NGINX proxy pool. No additional infrastructure to maintain.

File inspection and logging

When a file download matches certain criteria, a Worker can send the file to a third-party sandboxing service for detonation and analysis. Or it can write the file in its entirety to Cloudflare R2 as a permanent record for later inspection, without the file ever leaving the Cloudflare network.

Real-time alerting on policy match

A Worker bound to a Forward policy receives traffic whenever a specific selector matches. The Worker sends a message to a Slack channel or PagerDuty endpoint with the user's email, the rule that fired, and the destination URL.

export default {
  async invoke(ctx: GatewayContext, env: Env): Promise<void> {
    await fetch(env.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL, {
      method: "POST",
      body: JSON.stringify({
        text: `DLP alert: ${ctx.identity.email} triggered "${ctx.rule.name}" accessing ${ctx.request.url}`
      })
    });
  }
}

Complex evaluation logic

Traditional expression builders for firewalls are not designed for the kind of computation some organizations need at evaluation time. If you maintain internal risk scoring systems that perform behavioral analysis across multiple data sources, or if you have complex maps of users, groups, and conditional memberships where multiple criteria must be independently true, you can use a custom function as the computational extension that evaluates all of that logic and returns a single value to Gateway.

Performance and reliability

Because Gateway and Workers services run on the same machines in the Cloudflare network, dispatching to a Worker does not introduce a network hop. The performance impact is limited to the execution time of your Worker code itself.

When a custom function fails — throws an exception, times out, or returns an unexpected value — you configure the fallback behavior per function. Default values are required in the custom function contract, so that it’s easy to determine behavior.

Availability and pricing

The Forward action and its integration with Workers are available in a public beta starting today, with Custom Functions expected to be available before the end of the year. At general availability, both will be available for all customers on all plan types.

Traffic dispatched to your Workers is billed as standard Worker requests. The feature works with Workers Free, Workers Paid, and Workers for Enterprise with no restrictions on functionality. Workers Free does have execution time limits and daily request limits, which is worth considering as you scale the volume of Gateway traffic you send to your Workers.

DLP custom functions for inline detection validation

A fully programmable SASE platform extends beyond just Gateway. Our DLP offering — already integrated across Gateway, AI Gateway, Email Security, and more — now supports custom outcomes through integrations with our Compute platform, as well.

Most data security products operate by looking for data that matches known patterns. Customers can typically define regular expressions, word lists, or similar to operate these detections. They can also improve confidence in matching through the use of keywords or context analysis on the request body. But these methods have a core flaw: these types of detections can only tell you when something matches the pattern of data relevant to your organization, not whether this specific instance of data is indicative of data exfiltration or misuse.

As attackers become increasingly advanced, and agents can be used to ruthlessly exploit systems, improving our ability to accurately detect patterns is not enough. To improve accuracy for the data that matters, you need to know whether the data in question is actively relevant to your organization.

To solve this problem, most solutions leverage exact data match, but this comes with its own trade-offs. Customers must prepare, maintain, and transfer reference datasets, then decide how comfortable they are allowing a vendor to manage data from their most sensitive systems. 

Custom validation functions for DLP bridges that gap, and they’re available starting today. These custom functions allow customers to define their own validation logic, using their own source of truth, directly inside a Cloudflare Worker… and apply it everywhere they use DLP to protect their sensitive data.

Credential and secret verification

When a DLP detection entry is matched, an outbound Worker can be dispatched to run validation logic prior to a policy enforcement decision. If you have profiles to detect the use of GitHub secrets, but only care about active secrets, you can use a Worker to first look up the status of a detected key, return a response from the appropriate GitHub endpoint, and then decide whether or not the DLP profile should match the traffic.

import {
  DlpValidation,
  type DlpValidationInput,
  type DlpValidationResult,
} from "@cloudflare/zt-types";

export class DlpValidationEntrypoint extends DlpValidation {
  async validate({ excerpt, start, end }: DlpValidationInput): Promise<DlpValidationResult> {
    const bytes = Uint8Array.from(atob(excerpt), (c) => c.charCodeAt(0));
    const token = new TextDecoder().decode(bytes.slice(start, end));

    const res = await fetch("https://api.GitHub.com/user", {
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
        "User-Agent": "dlp-GitHub-validator",
        Accept: "application/vnd.GitHub+json",
      },
    });

    if (res.ok) return { score: 1.0 }; // token is valid and active
    if (res.status === 401) return { score: "veto" }; // token is invalid, discard
    return { score: 0 };
  }
}

What's next

This is just the beginning of the fully programmable SASE platform. We are actively working on increasing the entry points from which you can dispatch custom functionality to the entire Cloudflare One suite, with Email Security coming next. That doesn’t mean we’re done building: this new architecture will make it easier for us to build first-party features into all Cloudflare One services faster, more flexibly, and with improved developer experience.

It’s also getting easier every day to protect your Workers, agents, and their traffic using Cloudflare One. If you are an Enterprise customer who would like a strategy session for implementation, a preview of the coming functionality, or to be notified about the custom functions beta, please reach out to your account team.

Your organizational security can now do anything a Cloudflare Worker can do. We can't wait to see what you build.

  • Review the Gateway and Workers integration documentation
  • See example Worker scripts for use in Gateway
  • Teach your agent to build with Gateway and Workers
  • Learn more about Custom functions for DLP

item.title: Deploy with Void
item.description: Introducing Void: an open-source SDK, CLI, and self-hosted platform for building full-stack Vite apps and deploying them to Cloudflare.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Nakazawa
Michael Dong
item.content:encoded:
VoidZero's tools such as Vite, Vitest, Oxc, and Rolldown — bundled in one toolchain as Vite+ — have made frontend development faster, but building full-stack applications requires more than just a tooling stack. These applications need server routes, databases, local development environments, and a fast and easy way to deploy ideas to production.

We’re excited to open-source three new products that bring server routing, typed data access, and Cloudflare deployment into a unified Vite workflow.

  • Void Platform: A shared deployment platform for teams to host Void apps on Cloudflare.
  • Void SDK: A composable JavaScript SDK for building full-stack apps with Vite.
  • Void CLI: A CLI for provisioning resources and deploying Vite apps to Cloudflare.

The CLI deploys apps built with the SDK to the Platform. All three products are open-sourced as a single JavaScript package and Vite plugin that you can install via npm install void. With Void, you can build your server and client together, carry types from your database to the UI, and let Void automatically provision the Cloudflare resources that your app uses.

We originally set out to build a single, private platform for all users to deploy apps to. After VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we adjusted our direction to open-source the platform and allow anyone to install because we saw a growing need: companies want to encourage vibe-coded internal apps, but are concerned about security and do not want to give cloud access to every employee. Void addresses this problem.

Void Platform: a cloud platform for your company

The Void Platform is fully open source and you can fork it and adapt it to your needs by integrating your company's systems, customize deployment workflows, build features for your customers, or make it work on other deployment platforms. Use the platform as it is, contribute improvements upstream, or fork it and build only the features you need. The open source code can be used out of the box or as a starting point.

As an admin of a Void Platform, you control access, set resource limits, inspect deployments and usage through the Void CLI or admin dashboard, and provide guardrails so everyone else can ship serious and vibe coded apps to the same shared platform.

By installing a Void Platform, your team or customers have a shared deployment environment in your Cloudflare account on top of Workers for Platforms. Void Platform enables:

  1. Faster prototyping. Your team can quickly build prototypes, deploy them, and share working apps for feedback, without setting up a separate Cloudflare account or provisioning resources for every project. This reduces the time to ship internal apps from days/weeks to minutes.
  2. Non-technical teams building. This workflow also lets teammates who do not normally write code work with coding agents to build and share their own apps. A designer can create an interactive prototype, or an operations teammate can build an internal dashboard, then deploy it to the same platform. All with the right security measures in place.

To self-host a Void platform, you need:

  • A Cloudflare account with Workers for Platforms and R2 enabled
  • A PostgreSQL database
  • An account with your chosen login provider
  • A domain for your apps

Then install Void as a cloud platform by running a single command:

Once your platform is set up, approved users can connect to it via the Void CLI for deployment.

void connect https://api.orange-company.dev

A user builds their app using the Void SDK, which is what powers Void Platform benefits like authentication, framework detection, resource provisioning, and more. In other words, Void Platform only works because of the accompanying SDK and CLI.

Void SDK: zero-config infrastructure

Void turns a Vite app into a full-stack Cloudflare Workers app. You or your agents can write code and Void will automatically infer resource bindings and provision resources such as databases, queues, or AI bindings during deployment.

To get started, add Void as a Vite plugin:

import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import { voidPlugin } from "void";
import { voidReact } from "@void/react/plugin";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [voidPlugin(), voidReact()],
});

The Void SDK ships with adapters for popular JavaScript UI frameworks such as React and Vue, provides file-based API routing, pre-rendering, caching, islands, and end-to-end type safety from the database to your UI.

All of Void’s features are optional and composable. Void integrates with existing application frameworks such as Vinext, React Router, SvelteKit, Nuxt, TanStack Start, and Astro. You can use those frameworks for routing and rendering, while Void handles resource APIs using Hono, migrations, deployment, and authentication with Better Auth.

Let's take a look at building a server-rendered page, with types inferred from the database query through to the client:

// pages/blog.server.ts
import { defineHandler, type InferProps } from 'void';
import { db } from 'void/db';
import { posts } from '@schema';

export const loader = defineHandler(async () => ({
  posts: await db.select().from(posts),
}));

export type Props = InferProps<typeof loader>;

// pages/blog.tsx
export default function Blog({ posts }: Props) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {posts.map((post) => <li key={post.id}>{post.title}</li>)}
    </ul>
  );
}

By importing void/db, Void provides a local database to your app during development and makes void deploy provision D1 automatically for you in production. This also works for using AI through Cloudflare’s AI Gateway: just by importing void/ai, everything is set up automatically for you.

// routes/api/decide.ts
import { defineHandler } from 'void';
import { ai } from 'void/ai';

export const POST = defineHandler(async (c) => {
  const { question } = await c.req.json();
  const result = await ai.run('@cf/cloudflare/clef', {
    model: 'clef',
    state: {},
    questions: {
      decision: { type: 'noul', instructions: question },
    },
  });
  const probability = result.answers.decision.noul;
  return c.json({
    answer: probability >= 0.5 ? 'yes' : 'no',
    probability,
  });
});

Void's React router is built for Async React, using transitions and Suspense to enable responsive navigation across screens. When you pair this router with a modern data framework such as fate and UI libraries such as Astryx, you can coordinate navigation, data fetching and mutations through React's transitions, as well as actions and optimistic updates across your entire application. Together, these pieces let you build apps that feel synchronous on fast networks, gracefully fall back on slower ones, and keep interactions responsive during expensive rendering updates.

If a user does not need Void Platform’s team management features, they can use their own Cloudflare account. Void SDK also deploys to Cloudflare directly.

Void CLI: one deployment command

The Void CLI is the main interface for Void. The CLI manages the platform and deploys the app. It's built on top of the new cf CLI and works well with agents.

With the Void CLI, you can ask your agent to debug failing requests, read deployment logs, analyze how your app is performing, or have them take care of the full lifecycle by deploying a finished app for you.  

Once your app is ready to deploy to Cloudflare, you can run:

The first time you run void deploy, the CLI will prompt you to log into your Cloudflare account. Void builds your app using Vite, applies migrations, automatically provisions resources, and deploys to Cloudflare or a Void Platform. It can be used to handle the full lifecycle of your project such as building, deploying, and managing your resources and projects, for example:

Similar to how the CLI, and an agent by extension, can manage the entire lifecycle of a Void app, you can also use the CLI to manage a Void Platform:

  • Manage users, project access, and resources
  • Inspect deployments, logs, and rollbacks
  • Monitor platform health and usage

Connect with us

VoidZero’s mission is to make JavaScript developers more productive than ever before. We brought Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, Oxfmt, and Vitest together in Vite+ for development, bundling, code quality, and testing. Void extends that stack to full-stack application development, letting you and your agents build, test, and deploy entire applications.

We’ve been using the Void SDK, CLI, and Platform in production at VoidZero for the past several months and we are excited to see what you'll build with Void. Please share your feedback with us:

  • Discord: Step into the Void community Discord server for real-time discussions
  • GitHub: Star the repo, start discussions, and report issues
  • Deploy an app with Void: Quick Start Guide
  • X / Bluesky: Follow VoidZero for updates on X or on Bluesky

item.title: Cloudflare and OpenAI: Making AI discovery better for everyone
item.description: How Cloudflare and OpenAI are working together to help AI find useful content, keep up with changes, and make fewer wasted requests — making the experience better for users and website owners alike.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Conroy
Jack Galilee
Henry Aspegren (OpenAI)
James Balfour (OpenAI)
item.content:encoded:
Optimizing your site for AI is of little use if AI can't find it. The answer to someone's question may already be on your website: the installation guide you spent a week writing, or a first-hand account of using a product, with the details that make the difference for whether they buy it. As more people turn to AI for help, you want those systems to find your work, represent it accurately, and send interested people your way. You also want control over how they access your site.

Cloudflare and OpenAI launched a research pilot in July 2026 with those interests in mind. We wanted to find out whether signals from Cloudflare’s network could help ChatGPT users discover new content more efficiently.

Today, we’re sharing early results. So far, the answer is a resounding yes: the pilot has brought previously unknown pages into OpenAI’s search index, giving ChatGPT more sources to draw on to help people find relevant, timely information. Along the way, we’ve learned more about what makes a page worth discovering and how AI systems use the web.

Finding more of the web

The web is full of specifics. Someone fixing a washing machine needs the manual for their exact model. Someone applying for a passport needs the current requirements and fees. Someone choosing a local restaurant needs its latest menu and opening hours. Finding the right page can be the difference between a wrong answer and one that actually helps. These pages can be valuable even if few other sites link to them.

In the previous version of the web, discoverability was getting to the top of a search result page. It was then up to the human who visited your page to determine the value of the information, book that table, apply for that passport. As people increasingly rely on AI to find information and complete tasks, discoverability matters in new ways. AI systems need to find the right sources, understand what's useful, and connect people with relevant information – whether that's through an answer, a citation, or a visit to the website itself.

Cloudflare's network provides signals that can help OpenAI’s search crawler discover more useful pages across the web to surface to ChatGPT users. OpenAI then independently evaluates and ranks how those pages appear based on how relevant and helpful they are. Together, this creates a feedback loop that can improve both discovery and the quality of information people find.

This joint pilot, which used a participating cohort of ~1% of Cloudflare’s total network, has enabled OpenAI to discover and index hundreds of millions of new web pages, helping people discover more useful content and get more questions answered through ChatGPT. By linking back to relevant sources, ChatGPT Search also gives people a way to explore the original content and discover the websites and publishers behind it.

With GPT-6 and Intelligent UI, OpenAI is also making ChatGPT an even better place to shop, learn, and find answers, with more visual, interactive experiences tailored to what people need. This work complements these advances by helping ChatGPT discover more useful, up-to-date information from across the web.

From discovery to useful answers

Finding a URL is only the start. We need to know whether it leads to a page someone can access, whether that page offers anything distinct, and what it might help someone do.

We’ve learned, for example, how easily automated traffic can make a nonexistent page look interesting. Bots repeatedly ask for files that aren’t there. Some sites redirect almost any address to their homepage. Other addresses lead to copies of the same content. Recognizing these patterns gives us a way to cut wasted work before a crawler fetches the page, and improve efficiency in a way that benefits site owners.

We're also testing signals that identify and flag potentially harmful pages, adding another layer of information to support safer, more reliable discovery. A legitimate site can have a single compromised page, such as a fake login form planted by an attacker. Flagging that one page, rather than the whole domain, keeps people safe without penalizing the site owner. Early results suggest these signals can help identify pages that should be kept out of an index.

Making discovery easier

As more people use AI to discover information, website owners have new opportunities to reach interested audiences. For those who choose to make their content available to AI systems, these improvements make discovery easier and more efficient.

Keeping up by fetching every page more often would be expensive for everyone. For a website owner, a crawler that repeatedly downloads an unchanged page adds load without bringing any benefit.

The signals above are how we avoid that. Filtering keeps crawlers away from pages that don't exist or that redirect elsewhere. Change signals tell them when a page is worth another visit, and when it isn't.

There's a balance to get right. Finding new pages can initially increase crawling as those pages are evaluated and indexed. The goal is to keep discovering and stay current while reducing the work that takes. For Cloudflare customers, that means less unnecessary load. For OpenAI, it means more of its search resources are spent on information that helps people.

Making it worthwhile to participate

The next phase will build on what we’ve learned: improve the selection of pages, test faster and more reliable change signals, and measure what happens after content is discovered.

We’re continuing to work with OpenAI to understand how better site discovery can translate into real business outcomes, and we’ll keep sharing what we learn along the way.

Domain owners’ choices matter throughout. A signal about a page doesn’t grant permission to access it. This research uses metadata about the web for search and discovery, rather than sharing page content for model training.

You can use Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control to understand and manage how AI systems access your website.

item.title: Yandex outage: Data shows that instead of going dark, malicious bots went on the move
item.description: When strikes hit Yandex data centers, many assumed Russian bot operations went dark. Cloudflare data reveals that while search crawling stopped, malicious bots simply migrated to other networks.
item.dc:creator: Marina Elmore
Lai Yi Ohlsen
item.content:encoded:
Following reported strikes on Yandex data centers, claims circulated on the Internet that Russian bot farms and influence operations had been knocked offline. HTTP traffic charts showed steep drops, fueling speculation that the infrastructure damage had stopped these malicious actors. However, aggregate traffic metrics can easily mislead. There are two autonomous system numbers (ASNs) associated with Yandex: AS13238 is used by Yandex’s search engine, while AS200350 runs its cloud services.

Using Cloudflare Radar and Bot Management data, we analyzed how these two ASNs were affected — and while both saw drops in traffic, they saw differing impact.

  • Yandex Search (AS13238): The drop in traffic consisted almost entirely of verified search crawlers indexing web pages, images, and site resources.
  • Yandex.Cloud (AS200350): There was a decline in malicious activities like vulnerability scanning and probing, but high-volume automation did not vanish — it simply migrated to other hosting providers.

While malicious traffic may originate from a particular provider, it does not necessarily tell us who is responsible for the traffic. Understanding why the strikes had little lasting effect on malicious traffic requires analyzing request behavior, rather than just overall traffic patterns.

What happened: the effect of the strikes and pre-event baseline

Between October 7 and 11, reported Ukrainian drone strikes hit three Yandex facilities in Russia, progressively knocking data centers and network capacity offline. As seen on Cloudflare Radar, this culminated in a near-total collapse of the Yandex network on October 11 when traffic plummeted to 99% below baseline for Yandex Search (AS13238) and 90% for Yandex.Cloud (AS200350). Despite a brief partial recovery, both networks remained disrupted through October 13, settling at 86-90% below normal baselines. (As of October 14 at 18:00 UTC, traffic is at 85% of normal.)

A drop in overall HTTP traffic only confirms that the network went down. It does not reveal whether malicious or evasive bots were disrupted. Looking at the pre-event automation baseline, we can see that before the strikes, automated requests accounted for 36.1% of all HTTP traffic observed globally across Cloudflare's network, and 35.8% of traffic from Russian IP addresses.

The outage had different effects on automated activity on the two affected ASNs because they served different roles.

Yandex Search ASN (AS13238) is used for search index crawling. Cloudflare classified 99.5% of its requests as automated, and 93.6% of its bot requests as Verified. Our analysis showed that traffic from this ASN indexed pages, rendered pages, and rendered images, which is consistent behavior for a search crawler. The Yandex Search ASN supplied about 7% of Russia-origin bot requests, and just 0.05% of the global total.

Yandex.Cloud ASN (AS200350) is a cloud-hosting network and carries a very different mix of automation. Approximately 95.0% of its scored requests were bots, but none of its observed bot requests were verified by Cloudflare. Yandex.Cloud’s bots looked more like software apps: nearly two-thirds of their requests sent data to websites, some identified themselves as JavaScript, Python, or Go programs, and a larger share went to software companies than Yandex’s search bots. The Yandex.Cloud ASN supplied about 2% of Russia-origin bot requests, and just 0.01% of the global total.

Impact of the event on overall bot traffic

"Bot traffic" refers to automated requests to websites on Cloudflare's network, such as crawlers and scripts, not necessarily activity on social media platforms. As Yandex’s networks lost capacity, their bot requests fell too. That was expected: nearly all traffic from Yandex Search and Yandex.Cloud was automated. While we saw the obvious drop in total traffic, we did not see any evidence linking a global disruption in malicious traffic to the drop in traffic from Yandex.

Russia-origin bot requests fell roughly in proportion to the Yandex traffic that went offline, since most requests from those networks were automated.

Impact on Yandex Search ASN (AS13238): less search crawling

The decline on Yandex Search ASN was almost entirely search crawling. Sampled requests showed that 78.1% belonged to verified YandexBot, 11.5% to YandexRenderResourcesBot, and 1.9% to YandexImages.

Among websites and services, the industry segment that saw the steepest drop was Publishing and Newspapers, where traffic from Yandex networks fell 44%. Approximately 90% of pre-event traffic to news sites from this ASN was YandexBot indexing articles, with 40.5% of Cloudflare customers returning HTTP 403 Forbidden responses because the site owner blocked the crawler. When the Yandex Search ASN went offline, customers simply saw less indexing from Yandex.

Impact on Yandex.Cloud ASN (AS200350): legitimate use and migrating malicious traffic

Yandex.Cloud displayed a completely different profile. Following the reported strikes, bot traffic from Yandex.Cloud fell about 40%. Several attack-like categories showed especially sharp declines. For example, WordPress plugin probing fell 90% and scanner-identified requests fell 93%. Interestingly (and tellingly), Cloudflare customer blocks on Yandex.Cloud traffic also fell 70% during the event period, suggesting that proportionately less malicious traffic was even hitting the Cloudflare WAF from this ASN.

The majority of traffic from the Yandex.Cloud ASN fell into two industry buckets: computer software and gambling. The computer software bucket was predictable for an ASN meant to host third-party applications and software integrations. In fact, we even saw that api.cloudflare.com is a top hostname for Yandex.Cloud request traffic. An overall majority of that traffic succeeded (requests returned 200s) both before and during the event, pointing to legitimate usage.

The gambling sector offers the clearest evidence that malicious automation relocated rather than disappeared. Nearly all of Yandex.Cloud’s bot requests were targeted at one gambling customer account, with traffic shifting among its hostnames. Immediately following the October 8 disruption, bot requests from Yandex.Cloud to this account dropped to zero. Simultaneously, identical requests began appearing from other Russian hosting ASNs, including Radist and Selectel. The incoming traffic maintained an identical fingerprint across providers:

  • The same JA4 TLS client fingerprint
  • The same uncommon request paths and HTTP headers
  • The same custom User-Agent strings

Overall, Russian bot traffic targeting gambling accounts remained essentially flat over the week, moving from 167.7 million to 170.1 million requests (+1.4%). The automation never stopped running; the operators simply migrated their workloads to alternate cloud providers once Yandex.Cloud became unavailable.

Across most industries, the share of bot requests from Yandex.Cloud returning any HTTP 4xx response fell. This is largely due to a drop off in the attack-like traffic mentioned above. This, in combination with the gambling customer analysis, shows that malicious traffic that was sending requests through Yandex.Cloud simply shifted its “services” to other providers after the service disruption.

Finally, when we analyzed social media traffic, we found no unexpected changes in traffic either from Russian-origin IPs (0.6% decrease in total traffic over the event period) or globally (1.2% increase in total traffic over the event period). We repeated the analysis on bot traffic hitting the “post”, “reply”, and “like” endpoints for a specific social media platform and similarly did not find an unexpected shift before or during the event period from either Russian-origin IPs (5.7% decrease in total traffic over the event period) or globally (1.1% increase in total traffic over the event period). Based on our assessment, the data does not appear to support the claims that the strikes crippled social media manipulation, though without further analysis with data outside of Cloudflare, we cannot conclusively say there is no connection.

What the data told us — and what it didn’t

When traffic from Yandex networks collapsed, speculation spread across the Internet that Russian influence operations and malicious botnets had suffered a crippling blow. Cloudflare data tells a different story: across Cloudflare's network, there was no evidence that the strikes knocked social media manipulation offline or otherwise disrupted malicious activity on the Internet. Instead, the data demonstrated:

  • Search indexing dropped. The overwhelming majority of the traffic that dropped from Yandex Search ASN consisted of verified YandexBot crawlers fetching news articles and web assets. The main impact was reduced content discovery in Yandex Search.
  • Malicious automation migrated instead of stopping. While vulnerability scanning and plugin probing temporarily dropped on Yandex.Cloud, high-volume operations quickly moved to alternative hosting networks.

A network disruption means that specific servers stopped sending requests, but it does not mean an automated threat disappeared. Cloud workloads are portable, so when a data center goes dark or an IP prefix gets blocked, operators can migrate their scripts to another provider in hours.

Our analysis here is a reminder that client ASN traffic volume is an unreliable proxy for interpreting automated bot behavior. Defending against automated threats requires inspecting request behavior, such as identifying shared JA4 fingerprints, monitoring anomalous request rates, and applying WAF rules to sensitive endpoints, regardless of which network the request originates from. Physical infrastructure is static, but malicious automation is built to move.

item.title: Inside Hyperdrive: How we solved a rare Hyperdrive MySQL caching bug
item.description: While adding MySQL support to Hyperdrive, we found a subtle protocol bug when caching query results. Here is how we tracked down a 0.001% rate error and made Hyperdrive MySQL generally available.
item.dc:creator: Pranoy Dutta
item.content:encoded:
Hyperdrive support for MySQL is now generally available (GA). Hyperdrive, Cloudflare’s database connection pooler for Workers, initially only supported Postgres. Since we announced the beta for MySQL protocol support last year, we have been working on making our MySQL handling as reliable as our Postgres support.

We’ve learned some things from building and running a MySQL connection pooler on Cloudflare’s network. It turns out that the difference between beta and GA is just 20 bug fixes in a trenchcoat.

During the beta, our goal was to validate that real-world customer usage hit our production availability target of 99.99%. We knew there were gaps in our reliability since we track how often client connections from a Worker end in an error related to Hyperdrive. In addition, we had feedback from customers in the beta that led to the discovery of a rare and subtle bug in our production environment. To convey the complexity of this particular bug, we first need to explain how Hyperdrive works.

What is Hyperdrive?

Hyperdrive is a distributed database connection pooler that connects Cloudflare Workers to SQL databases. Hyperdrive holds warm SQL connections open on our global network and shares these connections across many Worker requests. In addition to connection pooling, Hyperdrive can also cache common queries in our global CDN cache, reducing latency and load on the origin database.

Establishing a connection to a SQL database is expensive, taking a minimum of five network round trips. On a serverless compute platform like Workers, establishing a connection for each request would be impractical, both because of the amount of latency added to each request, but also because a large number of open connections can incur high per-connection resource costs. While MySQL fares better here than Postgres since MySQL doesn’t use an entire OS process per connection, a typical deployment can still run into resource issues with a large number of connections.

For more details, see our blog post introducing Hyperdrive.

A journey to stability

Some of the issues we ran into were small and easy to fix once reported. One of the first problems reported in the beta was that emojis written to the database were not being correctly returned. This was a bug related to character set encoding. Hyperdrive negotiates the encoding for the connection in the startup handshake, and we negotiate utf8 as the encoding. As it turns out, utf8 is a deprecated alias for utf8mb3 which is not all of UTF-8: it only supports 1–3 bytes per Unicode code point, while full UTF-8 has a max of 4 bytes per code point. To get all of UTF-8, we needed to change our handshake to use utf8mb4 , which fixed the emoji issue.

Another encoding-related bug occurred when we added connection cleanup via COM_RESET_CONNECTION. This is a lightweight MySQL command to clear any session state in a given connection, which is exactly what Hyperdrive needs to ensure that no session-level state leaks between checkouts. But adding this connection cleanup step caused encoding issues once again! It turns out that COM_RESET_CONNECTION does not reset the connection state to the character set encoding we negotiated at connection startup; it instead resets the connection to the server default. This means that after negotiating utf8mb4 on a MySQL server instance that defaults to latin1, once we run COM_RESET_CONNECTION, our connection now has an encoding of latin1. The fix is to always run a command setting the encoding to utf8mb4 after a connection reset.

A hard-to-find bug

During the beta, our highest-volume MySQL customer reported a small but consistent rate of empty query responses for which a non-empty response was always expected. We started the investigation by combing through all of our telemetry and understanding the user’s logic. Then we also increased the trace rate for this Hyperdrive instance, hoping to see the execution flow of this bug. We searched for network issues that could explain the issue — but nothing seemed to account for this behavior. This error occurred about 0.001% of the time, which made it very hard to find relevant end-to-end execution traces.

But we did have one clue: the bug only occurred on Hyperdrive instances with caching enabled. This made us suspect an issue with Hyperdrive’s MySQL caching.

Hyperdrive caching

To understand Hyperdrive's caching, we first need to talk about Hyperdrive's topology and how it interacts with the CDN cache. Every Hyperdrive instance has a split architecture with two nodes: a Client and an Endpoint. The Client node runs on the same machine as the user’s Worker, handles local caching (if enabled), and forwards queries to the Endpoint if needed. The Endpoint node holds the connection pool and is placed in the data center closest to the origin database. Each node uses the Cloudflare CDN cache local to the data center it is running in. Importantly, this means that if the two nodes are running in the same data center, they will share a cache.

Sharing the cache between Client and Endpoint is generally good for performance. We use a hash of the contents of the query’s wire messages with some normalization and store the result bytes in the cache. If a Hyperdrive Client running in the same data center as its Endpoint receives a request, and that Endpoint has recently cached the results of the same query, the Client can serve the response directly from the shared data center cache. To work correctly, this scheme requires that the same bytes are cached for the same response, whether stored by the Client or the Endpoint.

MySQL client/server protocol

Since we couldn’t get a direct trace of the issue, we decided to spend time looking at the MySQL client / server protocol. Perhaps we had an assumption about Postgres’ protocol built into our MySQL handling that was causing these issues.

The protocol describes how a MySQL client communicates with a MySQL server. This can be somewhat confusing in the case of database connection pooling since we have two components acting like clients and two acting like servers. The first client is the Worker using a MySQL client library, and it connects to the first component acting like a server, the Hyperdrive Client. The Hyperdrive Client connects to the Hyperdrive Endpoint which acts as a MySQL client connecting to the actual MySQL origin server.

This protocol starts with the Connection Phase where the MySQL client and the MySQL server agree upon a common authentication method and capabilities. Once a connection is established, the client and server begin the Command Phase, where the client sends commands (e.g. SQL statements) to be executed with the server responding and waiting for the next command.

Capabilities are exchanged during the Connection Phase to support protocol evolution while remaining backwards compatible. Each capability is a feature, like supporting compression during the Command Phase. The clients and servers must only use features which the other supports, otherwise a protocol desync can occur, leading to unexpected behavior.

This capability negotiation can be tricky for Hyperdrive, since Hyperdrive acts as a client to the origin database, and acts as a server to the Worker. To ensure that Hyperdrive can parse the messages from the origin MySQL server, Hyperdrive has a fixed set of capability flags which are used to communicate to the origin database. Since it is possible for Hyperdrive’s set of capabilities to be different from the Worker client’s set of capabilities, Hyperdrive needs to translate all origin responses encoded by its capabilities to the capabilities that the Worker expects.

While trying to debug this issue, we found that a popular MySQL client library for Node.js (mysql2) does not currently support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, which changes how result sets are terminated. Without this capability, the server sends an EOF packet between the column definitions and rows, then another EOF packet at the end of the result set. When CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF is negotiated, the metadata EOF packet is omitted and the final EOF packet is replaced with an OK packet. MySQL server 5.7.5 and later supports this capability, but the newer OK-packet behavior is only used when the client negotiates it.

While Hyperdrive does support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, it’s possible that the Worker’s MySQL driver does not. To handle this, Hyperdrive adjusts its behavior to support the capabilities that the Worker client driver expects. This means rewriting result sets to include EOFs and to translate all OK packets to EOFs when required. 

After days of looking through telemetry, documentation, and Hyperdrive code, everything clicked. We finally came across the last missing piece: a faulty assumption in our Hyperdrive Client caching code. We baked in an assumption when implementing the Client caching for Postgres: that we can cache exactly the bytes we wrote back to the Worker. While this was a reasonable assumption to make with Postgres’ wire protocol, it no longer holds due to the mismatch in MySQL capabilities. If a Client node is caching exactly what it writes back to the Worker, these bytes are in a different format than what an Endpoint node would be expecting. That’s because the Endpoint node is always working with Hyperdrive’s capabilities, while the Client node writes back bytes that are translated to match the Worker’s capabilities.

Now if we put all these clues together, we can understand scenarios where Hyperdrive can return a MySQL response encoded with the wrong capabilities, leading to the unexpected empty results and hangs. The bug occurs when both the Client and Endpoint are in the same data center, sharing a cache, and when one reads a value cached by the other.

Here’s a closer look at two such scenarios.

Endpoint caches, Client reads

  1. The Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for query Q. It gets back a response R from the origin server and caches response result bytes R_hyperdrive (Response encoded with Hyperdrive capabilities) into the shared cache.
  2. Client receives another request for query Q, checks the shared cache and finds R_hyperdrive.
  3. Client responds to the Worker with R_hyperdrive without translating to the Worker’s capabilities.

Once we found this type of failure mode, the fix was simple. We now make sure that we always write back a canonical version of the query result bytes in the cache encoded using Hyperdrive’s capabilities, no matter which node stored it. After releasing this change, the empty row problem went away — and our success rate for Client connections reached 99.99%.
